name: Darjeeling & Kalimpong
tagline: Tea slopes, toy trains and Lepcha hills
meta_description: Plan Darjeeling and Kalimpong: toy train, tea estates, Sandakphu trek, Kalimpong nurseries and villages, with honest INR costs for every budget.
summary: Darjeeling and Kalimpong are the West Bengal hills between Nepal, Sikkim and Bhutan, 1,200 to 3,636 m high. Go March to May or October to November for clear views of Kangchenjunga. Plan 5 to 7 nights: Darjeeling for tea and the toy train, Kalimpong for nurseries and monasteries, Sandakphu for the high ridge.
intro: The Darjeeling hills are a short climb from the plains. New Jalpaiguri station sits at about 100 m; three hours of hairpins later you are at 2,045 m on the Darjeeling ridge, with Kangchenjunga 74 km to the north. In between lie Kurseong, the tea gardens of the Kurseong and Darjeeling slopes, and the orange villages of the Riyang valley. East of the Teesta river, Kalimpong sits on its own ridge at 1,250 m, with Lava and Rishyap higher up in the forests that run into Neora Valley National Park.

This is a small hive with a long memory. The Lepcha people lived here before anyone drew a border. Bhutan held Kalimpong until 1865, Sikkim leased the Darjeeling ridge to the East India Company in 1835, and labourers from Nepal built the tea gardens, the roads and the railway. Today Nepali is the common language, Tibetan monasteries share ridges with Hindu temples and Scottish mission churches, and the tea is protected by India's first geographical indication.

We plan this hive for three kinds of trip. The saver trip uses overnight trains from Kolkata, shared jeeps from New Jalpaiguri, and government lodges or homestays, and it is honestly cheap: a long weekend can cost under ₹10,000 per person on the ground. The comfort trip uses a private car, a tea-country hotel and village homestays. The signature trip stays at Windamere, Glenburn and Taj Chia Kutir, with a private guide.

Timing matters more here than almost anywhere in the Himalaya. The monsoon, June to September, brings most of Darjeeling's 3,100 mm of annual rain and regular landslides on the roads. October and November give the clearest mountain views. March to May brings first flush tea and rhododendrons on the Singalila Ridge, with more haze. Winter is cold, dry and quiet, and the best time for Sittong's oranges.

story.title: From thunderbolt ridge to tea country

chapters.heading: The Lepcha ridge of the thunderbolt
chapters.text: Before the British arrived, the ridge belonged to Lepcha and Limbu communities who farmed and hunted in thick forest. The Lepcha call themselves Rongkup, the children of the Rong, and have their own language and script. Wikipedia's Darjeeling article records that Lepcha inhabitants knew the ridge as Dorje-ling, the place of the thunderbolt, and many local names still carry Lepcha roots: Kurseong may come from kurson-rip, a small white orchid, Mirik from mir-yok, a place burnt by fire, and Sandakphu means the height of the poisonous plant. Through the 18th century the hills passed between Sikkim, Nepal and Bhutan. Kalimpong was under Bhutan from about 1706, and a Lepcha chief, Gyabo Achuk, held the fort at Damsang near Pedong until Bhutanese forces took the area.

chapters.heading: A lease, a sanatorium and a tea bush
chapters.text: In 1829 two Company officers crossing the hills saw the crescent ridge as a place for British officials to escape the heat of Calcutta. In 1835 the East India Company leased a strip about 40 by 10 km from the Chogyal of Sikkim. Archibald Campbell, a physician made superintendent in 1839, began planting Chinese tea seed around 1841. The first Company experimental gardens, at Tukvar, Steinthal and Alubari, followed in 1852, and Happy Valley in 1854. By 1870 there were 56 gardens and some 8,000 labourers, most of them recruited from Nepal. They spoke Nepali with each other, and from their languages, customs and shared work grew the Indian Gorkha identity that defines these hills today.

chapters.heading: Two feet of track to the clouds
chapters.text: Until 1878 the journey from Calcutta took five or six days by train, ferry, bullock cart and palanquin. Then the railway reached Siliguri, and in 1879 work began on a 2 ft gauge line up the Hill Cart Road. It reached Darjeeling on 4 July 1881, climbing from about 100 m to over 2,200 m with loops and zig-zags instead of a rack. The Batasia Loop, below Ghum, was added in 1919. The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway carried tea down and summer residents up, survived earthquakes, landslides and an 18-month closure in 1988 and 1989, and in 1999 UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site. The steam engines still running are B-Class tanks built between 1889 and 1925.

chapters.heading: Kalimpong, wool and the road to Lhasa
chapters.text: After the Anglo-Bhutan War, the Treaty of Sinchula in 1865 gave the British the hills east of the Teesta. Kalimpong was then a hamlet of two or three families. Its position on the mule route over the Jelep La to the Chumbi Valley and Lhasa turned it into a trading post for wool, furs and grain, and Tibetan, Bhutanese, Marwari and Nepali traders settled along its ridge. Scottish missionaries opened schools; Dr Graham's Homes started in 1900 with six children. The Jelep La closed after the 1962 war and the trade ended, but monks who came from Tibet after 1959 built monasteries, and Kalimpong's growers turned to flowers. Its nurseries still ship orchids, bulbs and cacti across India.

highlights.title: Ride the toy train to Ghum and Batasia
highlights.text: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999, still runs 2 ft gauge trains along the Hill Cart Road. The joy ride from Darjeeling climbs to Ghum, the summit of the line at about 2,260 m, and loops around the Batasia memorial garden. Steam rides cost more and sell out first.

highlights.title: Walk a working tea garden in first flush
highlights.text: Darjeeling tea has been a geographical indication since 2004, the first in India. From March to May the estates pluck the first flush, two leaves and a bud by hand. Happy Valley, 3 km from town, is open to visitors, and estates around Kurseong offer walks and tastings where tours run.

highlights.title: Watch Everest from Sandakphu
highlights.text: At 3,636 m, Sandakphu is the highest point in West Bengal. From the summit village you can see Everest, Lhotse, Makalu and Kangchenjunga on a clear morning. Walk up the Singalila Ridge in four days with a guide, or ride a vintage Land Rover from Manebhanjan.

highlights.title: Kalimpong nurseries and monasteries
highlights.text: Kalimpong's nurseries grow orchids, gladioli, bulbs and cacti for buyers across India. Spend a morning in the greenhouses, then climb Durpin Hill to Zang Dhok Palri Phodang, consecrated by the Dalai Lama in 1976, which keeps the 108 volumes of the Kangyur brought out of Tibet.

highlights.title: Sleep in a forest village above Lava
highlights.text: Lava, at about 2,195 m, is the gateway to Neora Valley National Park, where red pandas live in the bamboo and oak forest. Ten kilometres on, Rishyap faces the Kangchenjunga range from 2,590 m. Lepcha and Sherpa families run simple homestays with wood stoves and home cooking.

highlights.title: Orange season in Sittong
highlights.text: In the Riyang valley below Kurseong, Sittong's farmers grow Darjeeling mandarin oranges between their houses. From late November to January the trees are heavy with fruit. Stay in a homestay, walk the orchards, and visit Rabindra Bhavan at Mungpoo, where Tagore stayed between 1938 and 1940.

money_savers: Take an overnight sleeper from Kolkata to New Jalpaiguri instead of flying to Bagdogra; a sleeper berth costs about ₹500–700 and saves a hotel night.
From NJP or Siliguri, a shared jeep seat to Darjeeling or Kalimpong costs about ₹250–400, against ₹3,000–4,000 for a reserved car.
Book the diesel toy train joy ride instead of the steam one if budget matters; it covers the same Ghum and Batasia loop for less.
Share a Tiger Hill jeep with other travellers from your hotel; the per-seat fare is a fraction of a private booking.
Eat momos, thukpa and thali in local cafes off the Mall and Chowrasta, where a full meal costs ₹150–300.
Visit in the shoulder weeks of early March, late November and December, when hotels in Darjeeling cut rates noticeably.
getting_there: Most travellers arrive at New Jalpaiguri (NJP) station or Bagdogra Airport (IXB), both near Siliguri at the foot of the hills. From Kolkata, overnight trains such as the Darjeeling Mail and Padatik Express reach NJP in 10–12 hours, and a daytime Vande Bharat runs from Howrah. Bagdogra has flights from Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai, Bengaluru and other cities. From NJP, Darjeeling is about 70 km and 3–3.5 hours by road via Rohini or Pankhabari; Kalimpong is about 70 km and 2.5–3 hours via Sevoke and the Teesta valley. Shared jeeps leave NJP station and Siliguri when full; NBSTC buses run from the Tenzing Norgay Bus Terminus. The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway runs between NJP and Darjeeling on some days, but it takes 7 hours or more and services change, so check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian citizens need no permits for Darjeeling, Kurseong, Mirik, Kalimpong, Lava or Rishyap. Foreign nationals also need no special permit for these hills, but carry your passport. On the Sandakphu trek, Singalila National Park charges a daily entry fee and requires a registered guide; the trail touches Nepal at Tumling and Kalipokhri, which Indian and Nepali citizens cross freely, and foreigners should carry passport and visa for checkposts. Neora Valley National Park needs an entry permit from the forest office at Lava and closes in the monsoon. Fees and rules change, so check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Darjeeling 2 to 9 °C, dry, frost; Sandakphu below freezing
months.summary: January is cold and clear. Darjeeling's mornings are around 2 °C and the air is dry, so mountain views are often sharp, though fewer days are as clean as November. Sandakphu can get snow and the Land Rover road sometimes closes for a day or two. Sittong's orange harvest is finishing and Kalimpong's nurseries are quiet. Hotels drop rates after New Year, and the town belongs to locals again.
months.tip: Pack a down jacket and thermals; most budget rooms have no central heating.

months.weather: Darjeeling 4 to 11 °C, mostly dry, some haze
months.summary: February warms slowly. Losar, the Tibetan new year, usually falls in February or early March, and monasteries in Ghum, Darjeeling and Kalimpong hold prayers and dances. Snow is possible at Sandakphu and Lava. Tea gardens are still dormant; pruning is done and bushes are bare. A good month for quiet monastery visits and low hotel prices, with a fair chance of clear mornings.
months.tip: Check the year's Losar date before you book; it moves with the Tibetan lunar calendar.

months.summary: March is the start of the first flush. Estates pluck the first tender leaves after winter, and tea houses in Darjeeling start selling the season's lots. Rhododendrons begin to flower on the Singalila Ridge, and the Sandakphu trek opens properly. Haze from the plains starts to build in the afternoons, so mornings give the best views. Prices are still moderate before the summer rush.
months.tip: Ask for first flush by estate name and invoice number when buying tea; good shops show both.

months.summary: April is peak rhododendron season on the Singalila Ridge and a strong month for the Sandakphu trek. Tea gardens are busy with first flush plucking. Bengali New Year and school holidays bring more visitors from Kolkata in the second half of the month. Mornings are often clear and afternoons cloud over. Book toy train seats and Darjeeling hotels early.
months.tip: Start Sandakphu trek days by 7 am to walk before afternoon cloud and rain showers.

months.summary: May is the busiest month. Plains heat sends families uphill, Darjeeling's Mall is crowded and traffic jams on the Hill Cart Road are common. The second flush begins in late May, with the muscatel teas Darjeeling is known for. Pre-monsoon storms arrive in the afternoons. Villages like Takdah, Sittong and Rishyap stay calmer and cheaper than the towns.
months.tip: Avoid driving into Darjeeling on Friday evenings in May; leave NJP before 10 am.

months.summary: The first half of June is still busy with school holidays; the monsoon usually reaches the hills by mid-June and rain rises sharply. Second flush plucking continues. Views of the snow peaks become rare, but the forests turn very green. Landslides start to block roads. Neora Valley National Park closes for the monsoon, and Sandakphu treks wind down.
months.tip: Keep a spare day in your plan from mid-June for landslide delays.

months.summary: July is the wettest month and we do not recommend it for a first visit. Rain falls most days, fog hides the mountains, and landslides close roads between Siliguri, Darjeeling and Kalimpong for hours or days. Tea gardens pluck the monsoon flush, mostly used for blends. Hotels are cheap and towns are quiet if you must go. National parks are closed.
months.tip: If you travel in July, stay in one town and carry rain gear with sealed bags for electronics.

months.weather: Darjeeling 15 to 19 °C, heavy rain, leeches in forest
months.summary: August is as wet as July. Forest walks bring leeches, and the National Highway 10 along the Teesta, the main road to Kalimpong, is prone to slides. Toy train services may be cut back after damage. If you come, stay in Darjeeling town and use the cafes, museums and monasteries. Mountain views are very unlikely.
months.tip: Check road status for NH10 before any trip to Kalimpong in August.

months.weather: Darjeeling 14 to 19 °C, rain easing late in month
months.summary: Rain eases through September and the first clear mornings return towards the end of the month. Dashain often begins in late September or October, and Durga Puja holidays bring a large wave of visitors from Bengal. Hotels fill fast around the puja dates. Neora Valley National Park reopens mid-month, check current status before you travel.
months.tip: Book Puja-week rooms and trains two to three months ahead.

months.summary: October is one of the two best months. The monsoon has washed the air, and Kangchenjunga is often visible from Darjeeling and Kalimpong all morning. Dashain and Tihar fill the hills with tika, marigold garlands, lamps and sel roti. The autumn flush tea begins. Sandakphu views are at their sharpest. Expect crowds and high prices around the festival holidays.
months.tip: Be at Tiger Hill or any east-facing viewpoint by 5 am for the clearest light.

months.summary: November is our favourite month. Skies are clear most days, crowds thin after the festivals, and the autumn flush is on sale. Tihar often falls in late October or November. Sandakphu nights drop below freezing but the views of Everest and Kangchenjunga are excellent. Sittong's oranges ripen from late November, and village homestays are at their best.
months.tip: Pack for both 15 °C afternoons and sub-zero nights if you are going to Sandakphu.

months.summary: December is cold, dry and often clear. Christmas and New Year bring a short peak in Darjeeling, with prices rising for the last ten days. Sittong is in full orange season, and the Lava and Rishyap forests are cold and quiet. Snow can fall on the Singalila Ridge, closing the Land Rover road briefly. A good month for photographers who dress warmly.
months.tip: Book Christmas and New Year rooms early; outside those ten days December is quiet.

faqs.q: How much does a Darjeeling trip cost per person?
faqs.a: A saver trip costs about ₹2,000–3,500 per person per day for a government lodge or homestay, local meals and shared jeeps; a 3-night Kolkata long weekend is about ₹9,500 on the ground plus the train. Comfort trips with a private car and good hotel cost ₹6,000–11,000 a day. Signature stays at Windamere, Glenburn or Taj Chia Kutir run ₹20,000–45,000 a day. All figures are indicative 2026 and per person, twin sharing.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Darjeeling and Kalimpong?
faqs.a: October and November give the clearest mountain views, dry weather and festival colour. March to May is the second window, with first flush tea and rhododendrons on the Singalila Ridge, but more haze and bigger crowds in May. December and January are cold and clear. Avoid July and August, when heavy rain and landslides close roads and hide the mountains.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Darjeeling, Kalimpong or Sandakphu?
faqs.a: Indian citizens need no permit for Darjeeling, Kurseong, Mirik, Kalimpong, Lava or Rishyap. Foreigners need no special permit either but should carry passports. Sandakphu lies in Singalila National Park, which charges a daily entry fee and requires a registered guide. Neora Valley needs a park permit from Lava. Rules and fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I reach Darjeeling from Kolkata cheaply?
faqs.a: Take an overnight train from Sealdah or Howrah to New Jalpaiguri; a sleeper berth costs about ₹500–700 and 3AC about ₹1,300–1,800. From NJP, a shared jeep seat to Darjeeling costs about ₹250–400 and takes 3–3.5 hours. Book trains 60 days ahead for holiday weekends. The return works the same way, leaving Darjeeling by 1 pm to catch an evening train.

faqs.q: Is Darjeeling safe for solo women travellers?
faqs.a: Darjeeling and Kalimpong are generally considered safe for solo women, and many travel here alone. Shared jeeps are routine and drivers are used to tourists. Use normal care: avoid isolated paths after dark, book homestays through known operators, and share your plans when trekking. On the Sandakphu trek a registered guide is compulsory anyway. Local emergency number is 112.

faqs.q: Is the toy train worth it and how do I book?
faqs.a: For most visitors the 2-hour joy ride from Darjeeling to Ghum and back, via the Batasia Loop, is the best way to experience the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway. Diesel rides cost about ₹1,000 and steam rides about ₹1,500–1,700 per person. Book on IRCTC; seats open in advance and steam trains sell out in season. Timetables change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Will I get altitude sickness in Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Most people do not. Darjeeling is at about 2,045 m and Kalimpong at 1,250 m, below the height where altitude sickness is common. Sandakphu, at 3,636 m, is different: sleeping above 3,000 m can cause headache and breathlessness, so climb slowly over several days, drink water and descend if symptoms worsen. If you have heart or lung conditions, talk to your doctor before the trek.

faqs.q: Are there ATMs and mobile networks in the hills?
faqs.a: Darjeeling, Kurseong, Mirik and Kalimpong all have ATMs and good 4G coverage on major networks. Lava has limited ATMs; carry cash for Rishyap, Sittong, Takdah and Lepchajagat, where homestays often prefer cash or UPI. On the Sandakphu trek, network is patchy and sometimes Nepali networks are stronger than Indian ones. Carry enough cash for the whole trek.

faqs.q: Is Darjeeling good for families with kids and seniors?
faqs.a: Yes, with planning. Darjeeling town is steep and walking between the Mall, hotels and sights involves stairs, so seniors should stay near Chowrasta or use taxis. The toy train joy ride, the zoo and the tea gardens suit children. Kalimpong and Mirik are gentler. Avoid the Sandakphu trek for small children and those with heart conditions; the Land Rover ride is an alternative.
